sources.title: Book of the Dead
sources.author: Ancient Egyptian priests
sources.excerpt: I have not done evil to mankind. I have not oppressed the members of my family. I have not committed sin in the place of truth. I have not wrought evil. I have done no murder.
sources.longExcerpt: I have not done evil to mankind. I have not oppressed the members of my family. I have not committed sin in the place of truth. I have not known worthless men. I have not wrought evil. I have not done evil things. I have not caused the first consideration each day to be given to excessive labors as thy servant. I have not borne false witness. I have not defamed anyone. I have not slain man or woman. I have not done violence to any person. I have not stolen. I have not taken that which belongs to the temple. I have not uttered lies. I have not carried away food. I have not uttered curses. I have not committed adultery. I have not made anyone to weep. I have not eaten the heart. I have not attacked any man. I am pure, I am pure, I am pure, I am pure. My purity is the purity of the great phoenix which is in Heracleopolis. Behold, I am the nose of the Lord of Breath, who makes all mankind to live.

sources.title: Periplus of the Erythraean Sea
sources.author: Unknown Greek merchant
sources.excerpt: Beyond Opone, the coast trending more to the south, come the Small and Great Bluffs of Azania. There is the island Menuthias, low and wooded, where they catch tortoise in wicker baskets.
sources.longExcerpt: Beyond Opone, the coast trending more to the south, come the Small and Great Bluffs of Azania. After about four thousand stadia sailing along the Azanian coast, there is the island Menuthias, about three hundred stadia from the mainland, low and wooded, in which there are rivers and many kinds of birds and the mountain-tortoise. There are no wild beasts except the crocodiles; but there they do not attack men. In this place there are sewed boats, and canoes hollowed from single logs, which they use for fishing and catching tortoise. In this island they also catch them in a peculiar way, in wicker baskets, which they fasten across the channel-openings between the breakers. The inhabitants of this coast are men of piratical habits, very tall, and under separate chiefs for each place. There are imported into these markets the lances made at Muza especially for this trade, and hatchets and daggers and awls, and various kinds of glass; and at some places a little wine and wheat, not for trade, but to serve for getting the good-will of the savages. There are exported from these places a great quantity of ivory, and rhinoceros-horn and tortoise-shell.

sources.title: The Voyage of Hanno
sources.author: Hanno the Navigator
sources.excerpt: We passed a country burning with fires and perfumes; and streams of fire supplied from it fell into the sea. The country was impassable on account of the heat. We discovered a lofty fire larger than the rest, which seemed to touch the stars.
sources.longExcerpt: We passed a country burning with fires and perfumes; and streams of fire supplied from it fell into the sea. The country was impassable on account of the heat. We sailed quickly thence, being much terrified; and passing on for four days, we discovered at night a country full of fire. In the middle was a lofty fire, larger than the rest, which seemed to touch the stars. When day came, we discovered it to be a large hill, called the Chariot of the Gods. On the third day after our departure thence, having sailed by those streams of fire, we arrived at a bay called the Southern Horn. At the bottom of this bay was an island, having a lake, and in this lake another island, full of savage people, the greater part of whom were women, whose bodies were hairy. Our interpreters called them Gorillae. We pursued the men but could not catch any, for they all escaped to the top of precipices and defended themselves with stones. We took three women, who bit and scratched their leaders, and would not follow us. So we killed them and flayed them, and brought their skins back to Carthage.

sources.title: Ezana Stone Inscription
sources.author: King Ezana of Axum
sources.excerpt: By the power of the Lord of Heaven who has made me King, who reigns for all eternity, invincible to the enemy, I, Ezana, King of Axum and Himyar, of Raydan, of the Ethiopians and the Sabaeans, and of Silen, conquered the Noba. They boasted they would fight me. I burnt their towns, both those built of bricks and those built of reeds, and my people seized their grain, their bronze, their iron, and the images in their temples.
sources.longExcerpt: By the power of the Lord of Heaven who has made me King, who reigns for all eternity, invincible to the enemy, I, Ezana, King of Axum and Himyar, of Raydan, of the Ethiopians and the Sabaeans, and of Silen, conquered the Noba. They boasted they would fight me. I burnt their towns, both those built of bricks and those built of reeds, and my people seized their grain, their bronze, their iron, and the images in their temples. I destroyed the statues in their temples, their stores of wheat and barley, and their cotton. I cast their people into the Seda River. Many died in the water, the number I know not. I took prisoners, both adults and children. I came back to my royal seat, having conquered by the might of the Lord of the Land. And I set up a throne at the place where the rivers Seda and Takaze join, to the glory of the Lord of Heaven who has helped me and granted me dominion over all the lands. And I erected here a throne of stone in praise to the Lord of Heaven who is the master of all and has aided me to rule. May the Lord of Heaven give me strength and may He make my kingdom flourish.

sources.title: Account of Kandake Amanirenas and the Roman War
sources.author: Strabo (Greek geographer)
sources.excerpt: The Ethiopians, emboldened by the fact that a part of the Roman forces in Egypt had been drawn away, fell upon the garrison of three cohorts at Syene and took prisoners. They also sacked Elephantine. But Petronius, marching against them with less than ten thousand infantry and eight hundred cavalry, first forced them to flee back to Pselchis. He then sent ambassadors to demand return of what they had taken, and to ask why they had begun the war.
sources.longExcerpt: The Ethiopians, emboldened by the fact that a part of the Roman forces in Egypt had been drawn away, fell upon the garrison of three cohorts at Syene and took prisoners. They also sacked Elephantine. But Petronius, marching against them with less than ten thousand infantry and eight hundred cavalry, first forced them to flee back to Pselchis, an Ethiopian city. He then sent ambassadors to demand return of what they had taken, and to ask why they had begun the war. When they said that they had been wronged by the governors, he promised them that their complaints would be heard by Caesar. Meanwhile he marched to Pselchis. The Ethiopian queen at that time was Candace, a masculine sort of woman and blind in one eye. When she would not yield, Petronius attacked the city and took it after a sharp engagement. Then he advanced against the capital at Napata. Candace sent ambassadors to him and he finally made a treaty with her and marched back, razing the fortresses he had taken. Afterwards ambassadors from the Ethiopians came to meet Augustus at Samos, and he gave them everything they asked for, even remitting the tribute which he had imposed.

sources.title: Histories: On the Ethiopians
sources.author: Herodotus
sources.excerpt: The Ethiopians are said to be the tallest and most beautiful of all men. They have customs unlike those of the rest of mankind. When they choose a king, they select the tallest and strongest man among them.
sources.longExcerpt: The Ethiopians are said to be the tallest and most beautiful of all men. They have customs unlike those of the rest of mankind. When they choose a king, they select whichever citizen they judge to be the tallest man among them, and the one best suited by his strength to the kingly office. For burial, they preserve their dead in gypsum, after they have first dried the corpse. When they have done this, they paint the whole body over so that it resembles the living man as closely as possible. Then they set it within a hollow crystal pillar. The crystal is dug up in great abundance in their country, and is very easy to work. You may see the corpse through the pillar within which it stands, and it neither gives out any unpleasant smell, nor is it in any respect unsightly, though every part is as plainly visible as if the body were bare. They keep it in their houses for a full year, offering it the first-fruits and sacrificing to it. After the year is out, they bear it forth and set it up near the city. There is a meadow near their city where they say a table is set out by night full of all manner of roasted meats. This table, they say, is filled by the government, and any citizen may come and eat. The natives call this the Table of the Sun.

sources.title: Victory Stela of Piye
sources.author: King Piye of Kush
sources.excerpt: I sailed downstream to overthrow the rebels against the King of Upper and Lower Egypt. Every city I approached shook with terror. I opened every fortified gate. I fought in the battlements. I killed all whom I found who raised weapons against me. I made great slaughter among them and there was none who stood before me. Now when His Majesty arrived at Memphis, he found the water had risen to the very walls of the city.
sources.longExcerpt: I sailed downstream to overthrow the rebels against the King of Upper and Lower Egypt. Every city I approached shook with terror. I opened every fortified gate. I fought in the battlements. I killed all whom I found who raised weapons against me. I made great slaughter among them and there was none who stood before me. Now when His Majesty arrived at Memphis, he found the water had risen to the very walls of the city. Ships were moored at the walls of Memphis. Then His Majesty saw that it was strong, the wall raised high with new construction, and battlements manned in strength. No way was found to assault it. Then His Majesty was enraged at it like a panther. He said: 'By the life of Re, who loves me, by the favor shown me by my father Amon-Re, I shall take this city like a flood of water! I shall command the water to rise against it.' That night His Majesty ordered his soldiers to embark in ships and attack the harbor. They mounted the walls of Memphis from the ships and slaughtered many without number and brought prisoners to the place where His Majesty was. When morning came, His Majesty sent soldiers in to destroy those who had resisted. His people seized their horses, their ships, their treasures.

sources.title: Archaeological Record of Nok Culture
sources.author: Nok Culture (archaeological evidence)
sources.excerpt: The terracotta sculptures depict human figures with elaborate hairstyles and ornaments, evidence of sophisticated artistry.
sources.longExcerpt: The Nok culture of central Nigeria (c. 1000 BCE - 300 CE) produced remarkable terracotta sculptures that represent the earliest known figurative art in sub-Saharan Africa. The sculptures depict human figures with elaborate hairstyles, jewelry, and body ornamentation, showing hierarchical society with distinct social classes. Archaeological evidence indicates the Nok people practiced iron smelting as early as 500 BCE, making them among Africa's earliest iron-working cultures. The settlements show evidence of agriculture (pearl millet and oil palm), suggesting a stable society that supported specialized craft production. While we have no written records from the Nok, their material culture reveals a sophisticated civilization that influenced later West African cultures.

sources.title: The Conversion of Ethiopia
sources.author: Rufinus of Aquileia
sources.excerpt: Two youths from Tyre, Frumentius and Aedesius, were traveling when their ship put in at a port. The local people attacked and killed all aboard except these two boys, who were studying under a tree at some distance.
sources.longExcerpt: Two youths from Tyre, Frumentius and Aedesius, were traveling with their tutor Meropius on a voyage to India. When their ship put in at a certain port for provisions, the local people attacked the ship and killed all aboard except these two boys, who were studying under a tree at some distance. The boys were brought to the King of the Ethiopians. The King, discerning their intelligence, made Frumentius his treasurer and keeper of his records, and made Aedesius his cupbearer. When the King died, the Queen begged them most earnestly to remain and help her govern the kingdom until her young son Ezana should come of age. During this time, Frumentius began to search out with great care the Christians who lived among the Roman merchants. He encouraged them and urged them to establish prayer-houses in the various localities where they did business. When Ezana grew to manhood and took the throne, Frumentius asked permission to return home. The Queen and her son released him with great honor. Frumentius went to Alexandria and laid the whole matter before Bishop Athanasius, asking him to look out for some worthy man to send as bishop to the Ethiopians. Athanasius, having considered the matter and perceiving the wisdom of Frumentius, declared: 'What other man shall we find in whom the Spirit of God is as in you? You yourself must return, for you have been ordained by God.' He then consecrated Frumentius as bishop and sent him back to Ethiopia, where he brought King Ezana and his kingdom to the faith.

sources.title: Royal Pyramids of Meroe
sources.author: Kushite civilization (archaeological evidence)
sources.excerpt: The pyramids of Meroe stand as monuments to Kushite royalty, smaller and steeper than their Egyptian counterparts. More than 200 pyramids were built in this royal necropolis between 300 BCE and 350 CE. Each pyramid contained a chapel decorated with reliefs showing the deceased ruler making offerings to the gods, receiving the crown from Isis and Hathor, and being protected by Anubis. The burial chambers beneath held gold jewelry, bronze vessels, faience amulets, and objects inscribed in Meroitic script - a writing system we have yet to fully decipher.
sources.longExcerpt: The pyramids of Meroe stand as monuments to Kushite royalty, smaller and steeper than their Egyptian counterparts, with angles averaging 70 degrees compared to Egypt's 50 degrees. More than 200 pyramids were built in this royal necropolis between 300 BCE and 350 CE, housing the remains of kings, queens, and elite officials of the Kingdom of Kush. Each pyramid contained a chapel decorated with reliefs showing the deceased ruler making offerings to the gods Amun and Osiris, receiving the crown from goddesses Isis and Hathor, and being protected by the jackal-headed god Anubis. The burial chambers beneath held gold jewelry with intricate granulation work, bronze vessels, faience amulets depicting Egyptian deities, and objects inscribed in Meroitic script - a writing system derived from Egyptian hieroglyphs but representing the Kushite language, which we have yet to fully decipher. Archaeological excavations have revealed that Meroe was a major center of iron production, with massive slag heaps indicating industrial-scale smelting. The city controlled trade routes between the African interior and the Mediterranean world, exporting gold, ivory, ebony, and exotic animals while importing wine, olive oil, and luxury goods from Egypt and Rome.

citation.modernSource: Archaeological excavations by George Reisner (1920s) and modern Sudan antiquities

sources.title: Jenne-Jeno: Ancient Urban Settlement
sources.author: Ancient West African civilization (archaeological evidence)
sources.excerpt: Jenne-Jeno, located in the inland Niger Delta of Mali, reveals the earliest evidence of urbanism in sub-Saharan Africa. Founded around 250 BCE, this city covered 33 hectares at its peak and supported a population of over 10,000 people. Archaeological excavations uncovered circular mud-brick houses, iron tools and weapons, terracotta sculptures, gold jewelry, and glass beads from as far away as India and the Mediterranean. The city's wealth derived from its position at the crossroads of trans-Saharan trade routes.
sources.longExcerpt: Jenne-Jeno, located in the inland Niger Delta of Mali, reveals the earliest evidence of urbanism in sub-Saharan Africa. Founded around 250 BCE and continuously occupied until 1400 CE, this city covered 33 hectares at its peak and supported a population estimated at over 10,000 people. Archaeological excavations by Susan and Roderick McIntosh in the 1970s-1990s uncovered circular mud-brick houses arranged in clusters, suggesting extended family compounds similar to modern West African settlements. The material culture includes sophisticated iron tools and weapons (sickles, hoes, spearheads, knives), terracotta sculptures depicting human and animal figures with elaborate scarification patterns, gold jewelry including earrings and beads, carnelian and glass beads from as far away as India and the Mediterranean, and pottery showing technological evolution over 1,600 years. The city's wealth derived from its strategic position at the crossroads of trans-Saharan trade routes, where gold and slaves from the south were exchanged for salt from the Sahara and luxury goods from North Africa and beyond. No evidence of centralized political authority has been found - no palaces, monumental architecture, or royal tombs - suggesting Jenne-Jeno may have been governed by councils of merchants or elders rather than kings, challenging assumptions about how complex societies develop.

citation.modernSource: Excavations by Susan and Roderick McIntosh, published in 'Prehistoric Investigations in the Region of Jenne, Mali' (1980)

sources.title: Lydenburg Heads: Early Iron Age Terracotta Sculptures
sources.author: Early Iron Age southern African people (archaeological evidence)
sources.excerpt: Seven terracotta heads discovered in Lydenburg, South Africa, dating to approximately 500 CE, represent the oldest known Iron Age artworks from southern Africa. The hollow ceramic heads, some large enough to fit over a person's head, feature distinctive scarification patterns, elaborate hairstyles, and animal motifs including cattle and antelopes. These heads were likely used in coming-of-age ceremonies or initiation rituals. Their discovery alongside pottery, iron tools, and cattle bones reveals the beginning of Bantu-speaking farming communities in the region.
sources.longExcerpt: Seven terracotta heads discovered in Lydenburg, Mpumalanga Province, South Africa, dating to approximately 500 CE, represent the oldest known Iron Age artworks from southern Africa. The hollow ceramic heads range from small face masks to large helmet-like sculptures that could fit over a person's head, suggesting they were worn during ceremonies. They feature distinctive scarification patterns etched into the clay - parallel lines, chevrons, and cross-hatching that mirror body modification practices documented among later southern African peoples. The heads display elaborate hairstyles including crested ridges and topknots, and are decorated with animal motifs including cattle horns and antelope features, emphasizing the importance of livestock in early Bantu society. These heads were likely used in coming-of-age ceremonies or initiation rituals marking the transition from childhood to adulthood, or possibly in rain-making ceremonies given the agricultural focus of these communities. Their discovery alongside pottery, iron slag, tuyeres (clay nozzles for bellows), hoes, iron bracelets, and cattle bones reveals the arrival of Bantu-speaking farming communities in southern Africa, part of the Bantu expansion that brought agriculture, ironworking, and new languages across eastern and southern Africa between 1000 BCE and 500 CE. The sophistication of these sculptures, created just as these communities were establishing themselves in the region, demonstrates that artistic traditions traveled with migrating populations.

citation.modernSource: Discovered 1957, now housed in South African Museum, Cape Town

sources.title: Dhar Tichitt: Ancient Agricultural Settlement
sources.author: Prehistoric Saharan peoples (archaeological evidence)
sources.excerpt: The stone-walled settlements of Dhar Tichitt in Mauritania, dating from 2000-200 BCE, preserve evidence of the transition from hunting-gathering to agriculture in the Sahara. As the region desiccated, communities built increasingly complex dry-stone compounds with walls up to 4 meters high. Archaeological remains show they cultivated pearl millet, kept cattle, sheep and goats, and created pottery with elaborate geometric decorations. Over 400 settlements have been identified, forming one of Africa's earliest complex societies before being abandoned as the desert advanced.
sources.longExcerpt: The stone-walled settlements of Dhar Tichitt in southeastern Mauritania, dating from approximately 2000-200 BCE, preserve extraordinary evidence of the transition from hunting-gathering to agriculture in the Sahara during a period of increasing desiccation. As the once-green Sahara dried up, forcing communities to cluster around remaining water sources, they built increasingly complex dry-stone compounds with walls up to 4 meters high, creating fortified villages with populations ranging from 100 to 500 people. Archaeological remains excavated by Patrick Munson and others show these communities cultivated pearl millet (Pennisetum glaucum), one of Africa's indigenous grain crops, using stone hoes and grinding stones. They kept cattle, sheep, goats, and possibly donkeys, as evidenced by animal bones and rock art. They produced pottery decorated with elaborate geometric patterns created using comb stamps and painted designs. Over 400 settlements have been identified across the limestone escarpment, forming a hierarchical system with larger sites apparently controlling smaller satellite villages - evidence of one of Africa's earliest complex societies. The settlements were eventually abandoned around 200 BCE as the Sahara's expansion made agriculture impossible, forcing populations to migrate south toward the Niger River valley, where their agricultural expertise may have contributed to the development of later West African civilizations including the Ghana Empire.

citation.modernSource: Archaeological surveys by Patrick Munson (1970s) and subsequent excavations

sources.title: The Great Obelisk of Axum
sources.author: Axumite Kingdom (archaeological evidence)
sources.excerpt: The stelae field at Axum contains over 120 giant obelisks, the tallest reaching 33 meters and weighing 520 tons - the largest single stone ever quarried and erected in the ancient world. These granite monuments, carved to resemble multi-story tower houses with false doors and windows, marked the tombs of Axumite kings. The largest obelisk collapsed during construction, but others still stand, testifying to the engineering capabilities of 3rd-4th century CE Ethiopia. The tombs beneath contained elaborate burial chambers with arched ceilings, filled with gold and ivory treasures.
sources.longExcerpt: The stelae field at Axum in northern Ethiopia contains over 120 giant obelisks erected between the 1st and 4th centuries CE, the tallest reaching 33 meters (108 feet) and weighing approximately 520 tons - making it the largest single stone ever successfully quarried and erected in the ancient world until it collapsed, probably during construction. These monuments, hewn from solid granite and transported from quarries 4 kilometers away, were carved to resemble multi-story tower houses with false doors, windows, and wooden beam ends meticulously sculpted in stone, reflecting the architectural style of elite Axumite palaces. They marked the tombs of Axumite kings and queens who ruled a trading empire that controlled the Red Sea commerce between the Roman Empire and India, exporting ivory, gold, emeralds, frankincense, and slaves while importing silk from China, spices from India, and wine and olive oil from the Mediterranean. The largest standing obelisk, 24 meters tall, remains in place, while another was looted by Mussolini's troops in 1937 and returned to Ethiopia in 2005. Archaeological excavations beneath the stelae revealed elaborate hypogeum tombs with stone-cut chambers, arched ceilings demonstrating advanced masonry, and galleries that once held bronze lamps, glass vessels, gold jewelry including intricate filigree work, ivory carvings, imported amphorae, and iron weapons. The engineering required to quarry, transport, and erect these massive monoliths, combined with the wealth of grave goods, demonstrates that the Axumite Kingdom rivaled Rome in power and sophistication during the 3rd-4th centuries CE.

citation.modernSource: Archaeological research by the Deutsche Aksum-Expedition and subsequent excavations

sources.title: Taruga Iron Smelting Site
sources.author: Nok culture (archaeological evidence)
sources.excerpt: At Taruga in central Nigeria, archaeologists discovered 13 iron smelting furnaces dating to approximately 500 BCE, providing evidence that sub-Saharan Africa developed ironworking independently, possibly without an intermediate Bronze Age. The furnaces, constructed from clay with stone bases, contained slag, tuyeres (clay blow-pipes), and iron ore. Radiocarbon dates place these furnaces among the earliest in Africa, contemporary with iron production in Meroe. This discovery challenged long-held theories that ironworking diffused to Africa from the Mediterranean, suggesting instead that West Africans invented their own smelting techniques.
sources.longExcerpt: At Taruga in central Nigeria, archaeologists discovered 13 iron smelting furnaces dating to approximately 500 BCE, providing crucial evidence that sub-Saharan Africa developed ironworking independently, possibly without passing through an intermediate Bronze Age as occurred in Europe and Asia. The furnaces, excavated by Bernard Fagg in the 1960s, were constructed from clay with stone bases, standing about 1 meter tall with internal diameters of 30-60 cm. They contained iron slag (waste material from smelting), tuyeres (clay blow-pipes that delivered air from bellows), partially smelted iron ore, and charcoal fuel. Radiocarbon dates from associated charcoal place these furnaces between 500-300 BCE, among the earliest in Africa, contemporary with iron production in Meroe (Sudan) but far to the west. This discovery revolutionized understanding of African metallurgy, challenging long-held theories promoted by colonial-era scholars that ironworking necessarily diffused to Africa from the Mediterranean world or the Middle East. Instead, West Africans appear to have invented their own smelting techniques adapted to local ores and materials. The Taruga site is associated with the Nok culture, known for sophisticated terracotta sculptures, suggesting that ironworking and artistic achievement developed together. The advent of iron tools - axes, hoes, knives - enabled more efficient forest clearing and agriculture, supporting population growth and the eventual rise of West African kingdoms including Ghana, Mali, and Songhai. Iron weapons also transformed warfare and political organization across the continent.

citation.modernSource: Excavations by Bernard Fagg (1960s), published in 'The Nok Culture in Prehistory' (1969)

sources.title: The Royal Cemetery at Kerma
sources.author: Kingdom of Kerma (archaeological evidence)
sources.excerpt: The royal tumuli at Kerma in Sudan, capital of the Kingdom of Kush before Napata, contained the burials of kings accompanied by elaborate grave goods and sacrificed retainers. The largest tumulus, K III, measured 90 meters in diameter and contained a central burial chamber with a bed covered in gold leaf, hundreds of sacrificed cattle, and the bodies of over 300 people - servants, soldiers, and concubines killed to accompany their king to the afterlife. These 'corridor tombs' demonstrate a powerful centralized state that controlled trade between Egypt and the African interior from 2500-1500 BCE.
sources.longExcerpt: The royal tumuli at Kerma in northern Sudan, capital of the Kingdom of Kerma before the Kushite capital moved to Napata, contained the burials of kings accompanied by elaborate grave goods and sacrificed retainers on a scale unmatched elsewhere in Africa. The largest tumulus, designated K III by archaeologist George Reisner, measured 90 meters in diameter and rose to a height of several meters, containing a central burial chamber constructed of mud brick with a vaulted ceiling. Inside lay a bed covered in gold leaf upon which the king's body once rested (since disintegrated), surrounded by hundreds of pottery vessels containing food and drink, ostrich feather fans, ebony and ivory furniture inlaid with gold, faience amulets, bronze weapons and tools, and jewelry including gold beads, carnelian rings, and lapis lazuli imported from Afghanistan via Egypt. The burial was accompanied by the systematic sacrifice of over 300 people - young men and women who were servants, soldiers, concubines, and possibly family members, arranged in rows in corridors radiating from the central chamber, their bodies positioned as if sleeping, waiting to serve their master in the afterlife. Additionally, hundreds of cattle were slaughtered and their skulls arranged in decorative patterns on the tumulus surface, demonstrating the importance of cattle wealth in Nubian society. These 'corridor tombs' or 'royal sacrifice burials' demonstrate a powerful centralized state with absolute authority over its subjects, controlling lucrative trade routes between Egypt and the African interior from approximately 2500-1500 BCE. Kerma reached its peak during Egypt's Second Intermediate Period when it briefly conquered southern Egypt, before being destroyed by the New Kingdom pharaoh Thutmose I around 1500 BCE.

citation.modernSource: Excavations by George Reisner (1913-1916) and Charles Bonnet (1970s-present)
